Ulam
YOO-lam
proper noun
Hebrew Ulam (H198), commonly read their leader or porch — from a root signifying what stands in front.

Biblical Definition

Two men named Ulam appear in the genealogies of Chronicles. The first is a Manassite, son of Sheresh of the house of Machir and Gilead, whose son was Bedan (1Ch 7:16-17). The second is a Benjamite of the house of Eshek, and of him the chronicler records something he records of almost nobody in these lists: the sons of Ulam were mighty men of valour, archers, and had many sons, and sons' sons, an hundred and fifty (1Ch 8:40). In a chapter of bare names, one household is singled out for two things together — skill in war and a great many descendants. The combination is not accidental in Scripture's way of thinking. The psalm says it directly: As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them (Psa 127:4-5). Ulam's house had both quivers, the literal one and the figurative, and Chronicles counts the second as the greater. A hundred and fifty sons and grandsons, all of Benjamin, is a small army raised in a household over three generations.

Origin & Era

The name of two men in the genealogies: a Manassite of the house of Gilead, and a Benjamite whose sons were mighty men of valour and archers.

ULAM, Hebrew Ulam, commonly read their leader, or porch.

1. A son of Sheresh, of the house of Machir and Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh.

His son was Bedan.

2. The firstborn of Eshek, of the tribe of Benjamin.

His sons were mighty men of valour, archers, an hundred and fifty with their sons.

Key Scripture

1Ch 7:16 — "And Maachah the wife of Machir bare a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem."

1Ch 7:17 — "And the sons of Ulam; Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh."

1Ch 8:39 — "And the sons of Eshek his brother were, Ulam his firstborn, Jehush the second, and Eliphelet the third."

Psa 127:3 — "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward."

Modern Corruption

Children are counted as a cost and a limit; Scripture counts them a heritage and an inheritance from the LORD.

expand to see more

The prevailing view treats children as an expense to be planned around — each one a subtraction from freedom, income and opportunity, and a large family as evidence of poor judgment. Chronicles thinks the other way, and says so by what it bothers to record. In a chapter of unadorned names, the household of Ulam earns a sentence because it produced a hundred and fifty sons and grandsons who could handle a bow. That is written down as an achievement, alongside valour in battle and in the same breath.

The doctrine is stated plainly elsewhere: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward (Psa 127:3), and the first commission given to man in an unfallen world was to be fruitful and multiply (Gen 1:28). This is not a promise that every marriage will be fruitful, nor a rebuke to those the LORD has not given children; Scripture is tender with Hannah and with Elisabeth. It is a correction of the accounting. The principle to recover is that a household raising children for God is building something that outlasts every other work a man does, and that the hundred and fifty of Ulam's line are recorded because heaven counts them.

Hebrew Ulam (H198), commonly read their leader or porch, from a root signifying that which stands in front.

Hebrew Ulam (H198) — borne by a Manassite and a Benjamite; 1 Chronicles 7:16-17, 8:39-40.

Hebrew gibbor chayil — a mighty man of valour; the description of Ulam's sons.

Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — a bow; the archers of Benjamin were famed in Israel.

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage; children are an heritage of the LORD (Psa 127:3).

Hebrew ashpah (H827) — a quiver; happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them (Psa 127:5).

"“Ulam his firstborn, Jehush the second, and Eliphelet the third”."
